svg.desc: Banner for a paper on the expected maximum of very rough fractional Brownian motion on the unit interval. A chart plots the exact first-order share of the true expected maximum that a uniform grid of n points captures, against c = H log n from 0 to 5, where H is the Hurst parameter. The blue curve is F(c) divided by the square root of 2: it equals the square root of c/2 up to c = 1/2 and then 1 minus one half of e to the power 1/2 minus c, rising towards 100 per cent. A dashed green line at 100 per cent marks the whole path, whose expected maximum times the square root of H tends to the square root of 2 (Theorem 1). A gold point marks half the maximum at H log n = 1/2 and a white point marks 90 per cent at H log n of about 2.11. A side panel says what this means for a simulation: a grid with n = e to the c over H points sees half at c = 0.5, 90 per cent at c of about 2.11 and 99 per cent at c of about 4.41; the first-order prediction at H = 0.1 is about 150 points for half and about 1.5 billion for 90 per cent. These are limits as H tends to zero; convergence is slow.
svg.text: How much of a rough random path’s maximum does a grid of points see?
Fractional Brownian motion with small Hurst parameter H: the answer depends only on c = H log n
c = H log n (H = Hurst parameter, n = grid points)
share of the true expected maximum seen by the grid
half the maximum at H log n = ½
What it means for a simulation
A grid with n = ec/H points sees, to first order:
Exact limit as H → 0; convergence is slow.
